sources.title: Hexadirectional coding of visual space in human entorhinal cortex
sources.authors: Matthias Nau; Tobias Navarro Schröder; Jacob L. S. Bellmund; Christian F. Doeller

rights.basis: Original curated summary and verified bibliographic metadata; no full article text reproduced.

answers.answer:
UNIVERSAL ONE
The paper found sixfold directional organisation in a human brain signal—not evidence that the brain implements M9 P24.

What the study found
Nau and colleagues used human fMRI during a controlled visual-tracking task. Entorhinal-cortex activity showed sixfold rotational modulation with gaze direction: a directional pattern repeating every 60°. This supports a grid-like representation of visual space. [1]

The important distinction is between the measurement—a population-level fMRI signal—and its interpretation as grid-like coding. The study did not directly image individual grid cells or demonstrate a literal hexagonal anatomical structure or tetrahedral eye mechanism. It did not test Fibonacci sequences, EMDR outcomes or quantum error correction. [1]

What connects to M9 P24—and what remains hypothetical
M9 P24 is a mathematical construction: Fibonacci residues modulo 9 repeat over 24 positions. Its primary Gamma nodes occupy indices 0, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20; on the Atlas circle, these form a regular hexagon. That geometry is a computed property of the sequence and plotting framework, not a biological measurement. [2][3]

The legitimate connection is therefore shared sixfold symmetry, which offers a research comparison. The following remain hypotheses:

- That entorhinal visual coding follows M9 P24 or its Alpha, Beta, Gamma or Epsilon sequences.
- That the Atlas hexagon and the fMRI pattern arise from the same physical mechanism.
- That this relationship explains biological timing, cellular division or molecular organisation in the OXTR programme. The Atlas records those biological links as hypotheses, with biological significance not yet assessed. [1][2]

A meaningful test needs a quantitative M9-specific prediction, comparison against alternative periodicities and independent neural data—not merely a resemblance between hexagonal diagrams. The repository explicitly identifies rotational-symmetry testing with competing periodicities and independent data as the relevant methodological bridge. [1]

Paper: Nau et al. (2018). *Hexadirectional coding of visual space in human entorhinal cortex*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: [10.1038/s41593-017-0050-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-017-0050-8). [4]

*Evidence limit: the repository provides a curated research summary and bibliographic record, rather than a complete full-text methodological account for this paper.* [4]

answers.question: In our research repository, explain The Penrose Tiling is a Quantum Error-Correcting Code and its Fibonacci tiling variants. State its publication status and compare it with Dynamically Generated Logical Qubits. Cite both.

sources.label: S1
sources.title: The Penrose Tiling is a Quantum Error-Correcting Code
sources.text: Li and Boyle construct quantum error-correcting codes from Penrose tilings and variants based on Ammann–Beenker and Fibonacci tilings. Their construction connects nonperiodic geometric structure with the ability to recover information after local errors or erasures.

sources.label: S2
sources.title: Dynamically Generated Logical Qubits
sources.text: Hastings and Haah construct a honeycomb code in which a repeating schedule of two-qubit measurements creates logical qubits. Information protection comes from the code and measurement sequence acting together on the lattice.

answers.answer:
UNIVERSAL ONE
The repository presents two distinct approaches to quantum error correction: nonperiodic tiling-based codes and dynamically generated honeycomb codes. Neither establishes that geometry alone protects a physical quantum device. [1][2]

Penrose tilings and Fibonacci variants

Li and Boyle’s *The Penrose Tiling is a Quantum Error-Correcting Code* constructs quantum codes from Penrose tilings, with variants based on Ammann–Beenker and Fibonacci tilings. The central mathematical connection is between nonperiodic structure, local indistinguishability and recovery after local errors or erasures. [1]

In plain language, local indistinguishability means that inspecting a limited region does not reveal which protected quantum information is stored. The information resides in the larger structure rather than in one locally readable part. Recovery is a property of the specified quantum code—not simply of drawing a tiling.

The Fibonacci variants extend this tiling-based construction; they are not the Atlas M9 P24 sequences. The repository does not index the paper’s full text, so its exact variant definitions, recovery procedures and resource requirements are not available for a detailed methods comparison here. Connections to M9 P24, Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Epsilon remain hypotheses. [1]

Publication status: the repository records this as an arXiv theoretical preprint, version 2 (2024), not peer-reviewed, with status reviewed on 26 October 2026. Its recorded source is [arXiv:2311.13040v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.13040v2). This is the repository’s recorded status, not an independent live publication check. [3]

**Comparison with *Dynamically Generated Logical Qubits*

Hastings and Haah’s paper is recorded as a peer-reviewed theoretical publication in Quantum (2021), DOI [10.22331/q-2021-10-19-564](https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2021-10-19-564). It constructs a honeycomb code whose logical qubits arise through a repeating schedule of two-qubit Pauli measurements. [S4]

The key distinction is:

- Penrose/Fibonacci: protection is established through the mathematical structure of nonperiodic tiling-based quantum codes, including local indistinguishability and recoverability. [S1]
- Honeycomb: protection depends on the lattice together with the measurement sequence and decoding**, not on passive hexagonal geometry. [2]

For our Quantum Atlas programme, these are theoretical benchmarks, not validations of our sequence preparations. The Penrose work is not an Aquila demonstration, and our current Aquila workflow does not implement the Hastings–Haah measurement-and-decoding procedure. Neither paper, as recorded, establishes that our Fibonacci or M9 preparations improve error correction. [1][2]
